summary:
The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct under its 2014 Penal Code, which extended the offence beyond Muslims to everyone, and reporting on the statute notes that death-penalty provisions remain theoretically in reach. Enforcement is documented rather than theoretical: police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men, aged 56 and 27, on 29 August 2015 after they were found engaging in homosexual activity in a private home.

The Dhaandhoo case matters for what it shows about reach. Prosecution extended into a residence on a local island, so the exposure is not confined to conduct in public spaces or to Maldivian nationals. Rainbow Warriors warned after the arrests that tourists could face similar threats.

The state's international legal position constrains available protections. The Maldives holds reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and the CRC, and UN review of those reservations records concerns including sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage. Within that framework the Human Rights Committee recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against the stigmatisation of homosexuals.

Human-rights measurement points the same way. In HRMI's 2024 second expert survey, experts most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people — alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers — as at risk of violations of empowerment rights.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 HRMI survey scores political participation in the Maldives relatively better, at 6.4 out of 10, while other civil and political rights score considerably lower. Institutions that record citizen input therefore function better than the machinery that would deliver a remedy to a person facing prosecution or stigmatisation.

Groups identified alongside LGBTQIA+ people as at risk of empowerment-rights violations include migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers. The pattern across these categories is one in which several minority and advocacy-facing groups encounter the same weak protection, rather than a position specific to gender or sexuality alone.

In its second-cycle Universal Periodic Review the government's own submission accounted for 126 first-cycle recommendations: 89 fully accepted, 11 partially accepted, 6 noted and 20 rejected with reasons, alongside claimed full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 over four years. The gap between acceptance and reported implementation is where the anti-discrimination recommendations sit.

The Rainbow Warriors warning issued in 2015 treats the Maldives as a threat environment for visitors, which places the Dhaandhoo arrests in a regional pattern of cross-border concern rather than an isolated domestic matter.
localsOnly:
Maldivian LGBTQIA+ people face prosecution under the Penal Code as amended in 2014, and the documented arrest of two men inside a private home on Dhaandhoo on 29 August 2015 indicates that charges can follow from conduct away from public view.

HRMI's 2024 expert survey places LGBTQIA+ people among the groups most exposed to violations of empowerment rights in the Maldives, and records political participation at 6.4 out of 10 against considerably lower scores for other civil and political rights.

The Human Rights Committee has recommended that the Maldives enact legislation covering discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and take action against the stigmatisation of homosexuals. UN review of the country's treaty reservations flags sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage among the concerns recorded.

The government's second-cycle UPR submission reports full implementation of 58 first-cycle recommendations and partial implementation of 32 over four years, out of 89 accepted outright.
outOfScopeNotes:
Gender identity is not addressed by any source in this inventory. Document and marker rules, gender-recognition procedure, entry and visa screening that could disclose a visitor's gender history, and the treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers are unresolved here, as is the penalty structure for gender nonconformity as distinct from same-sex conduct.

Whether resort islands are treated differently from local islands is not sourced in this inventory. The single enforcement example available is a local island, and no source in the inventory states either that resorts are legally exempt or that visitors there face equivalent risk.

The national UPR report supplies acceptance and rejection counts for 126 first-cycle recommendations without identifying which recommendations were rejected. Whether the Human Rights Committee's recommendation on sexual-orientation anti-discrimination fell within the 20 rejected is unresolved.

Hate-crime provisions covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and rules governing access to gendered facilities, are not sourced in this inventory.
